title: When a price only goes up

steps.title: Up 40% in a week
steps.body: A share jumps 40% in a week and everyone talks about it. It feels like it can only go up. But prices that rise fast usually fall fast too. These big swings are called [[volatility]].

stat.label: €10,000 after +40% one week and −40% the next

steps.title: The fall is taken from more
steps.body: €10,000 rises 40% to €14,000. Then it falls 40%, and 40% of €14,000 is €5,600. You end at €8,400: down 16%, although the rise and the fall were the same size.

steps.prompt: After a loss, how much must the price rise just to get back to the start? Find the loss that needs a +100% gain.

goal.hint: Think of losing half the money.

steps.title: Losses weigh more than gains
steps.body: Lose 10%, and you need 11% to get back. Lose half, and you need to double. The deeper the fall, the harder the climb. A fall from a previous high is a [[drawdown]].

steps.prompt: Why doesn't +40% followed by −40% bring you back to the start?
options: The −40% is taken from a bigger amount than the +40% was
The bank charges a fee in between
Prices always fall faster than they rise
steps.explanation: The second percent applies to the new, larger amount, so the same-sized fall removes more money.

steps.prompt: A share fell 50%. What rise does it need to get back to its old price?
steps.explanation: Half the money has to double to be whole again.

steps.title: Your savings account
steps.body: Your savings account holds **{savingsBalance}**. It does not swing at all. Money in a single share can fall 50% in a bad year, and then needs +100% to get back.

goal.hint: Try −50%: the money is cut in half.
